retrieval_candidates.document: Slide 13: Limitations No model is perfect, and Evo 2 has some important limitations. First, everything it produces—whether it's a harmfulness score or a newly generated DNA sequence—is only a prediction, not a medical decision. Any result that could affect patient care must still be tested in a laboratory or confirmed through clinical studies before anyone acts on it. Second, because Evo 2 can generate realistic DNA sequences, there's a genuine concern about misuse. The same technology that can be used for helpful applications in synthetic biology could also be misused. To reduce this risk, the researchers excluded viruses that infect plants, animals, and humans from the training data, making it harder for the model to help generate something dangerous. This is an important safety measure, but it doesn't eliminate all the risks, especially since the model is fully open. Another limitation is the amount of computing power needed to train a model like this. Training required over 1,000 GPUs and trillions of DNA letters, making it unrealistic for most universities or research labs to build a similar model from scratch. Finally, Evo 2 doesn't perform equally well on every type of gene or mutation. Independent studies found that its accuracy varies depending on the task, and some datasets contain far more harmless mutations than harmful ones, which can make the overall score look better than the model's performance on the rarer, more important cases. This reminds us that we should always look beyond a single accuracy score when evaluating an AI model. Now that we've covered both the strengths and limitations, let's look at where this research could go in the future. Slide 14: Future Directions The paper also discusses where models like Evo 2 could be useful in the future. In drug discovery, it can help researchers identify which mutations are worth testing, saving time and money. Because DNA contains the instructions for making proteins, Evo 2 could also support protein engineering by helping design DNA that produces proteins with useful properties. In synthetic biology, future versions may even help design entire genomes instead of just small DNA sequences. Another exciting application is personalized medicine, where the model could predict whether a person's unique genetic variants are likely to be harmful. Beyond biology, the StripedHyena 2 architecture could also benefit AI systems that need to process very long sequences, such as long documents, codebases, or videos. Looking further ahead, researchers also hope to build models that learn from DNA, RNA, and proteins together for a more complete understanding of biology

Slide 6: How Evo 2 Learns The training process works in a few simple steps. You start with a raw DNA sequence, just a long string like "...ATCGGCTA..." That string gets broken into tokens, one letter at a time. Remember, a token is just one small piece the model reads at a time. Unlike some language models, which group several letters together into one token, here every single DNA letter gets its own token — nothing gets squeezed together or simplified. The model then predicts the next letter, and that prediction gets compared to what the real next letter actually was, using something called cross-entropy loss, which is just a math way of measuring how wrong or right a guess was — it's the exact same method used to train language models. This process repeats at every single position in the genome, over and over, trillions of times, and the model is never told what a gene is or what a mutation is. It only ever tries to guess the next letter. Why does this actually work? First, no labels are needed. The correct answer here is simply whatever letter actually comes next in a real DNA sequence — and that's available in unlimited amounts, with zero human work needed to label it. Compare that to trying to build a list of "these mutations are harmful, these are not" by hand, which would take forever. Second, this forces the model to learn useful patterns along the way. To get good at guessing the next letter, the model is forced to quietly pick up real structure — things like codons, which are little three-letter groups that spell out instructions for building proteins, common patterns called motifs, and the "grammar" of how genes are controlled — even though nobody ever directly taught it any of these ideas. And third, this is basically the exact same method used to train large language models: try to guess what comes next, given everything before it. So here's what I want you to remember: Evo 2's training method didn't need any special biology knowledge to design. retrieval_candidates.document: Slide 7: Why Standard Transformers Are Not Enough Here's where we hit a real technical problem. Standard attention, the method used in regular transformers, works by comparing every single position in a sequence to every other position. That means if you double how long your sequence is, the amount of computer work goes up by four times, not two times — that's what's called quadratic growth, versus the much gentler, near-linear growth we want instead. That's fine for the sequence lengths normal language models deal with, usually a few thousand up to maybe a hundred thousand tokens. But it becomes completely unworkable once you're talking about a million tokens, especially when you're training a huge model on trillions of examples. And this really matters in biology, because the parts of DNA that control genes, and the connections between genes, can be spread hundreds of thousands, even millions, of letters apart. So if you want to catch these long-distance relationships, you genuinely need a model that can look across that much space at once — you can't just fake it with a clever shortcut. Put those two facts together, and you get the conclusion: at the level of looking at every single DNA letter, with a goal of a 1 million letter view, regular attention is simply too expensive to train, no matter how much computer hardware you have. This is actually the same wall that a lot of AI researchers have been running into with long text sequences too, which is why people have already built things like sparse attention, other efficient attention tricks, and convolution-based models like the earlier version of Hyena. Evo 2 builds on that same line of work, but has to push it even further, because DNA doesn't give you an easy shortcut the way language does — you really do need to look at every single letter, one at a time. So here's the real question: can we build a model whose cost grows slowly and gently as the sequence gets longer, while still being able to catch those important long-distance patterns, the way attention can? retrieval_candidates.document: Slide 1: Evo 2 — A Foundation Model for Genomic Understanding and Design Hi everyone, thanks for being here. Today I want to talk about a paper called Evo 2. It came out in the journal Nature in 2026, and the title is "Genome modelling and design across all domains of life with Evo 2." It was made by a big team, led by the Arc Institute and NVIDIA, along with Stanford, UCSF, Berkeley, and a few other groups. The main idea behind this whole talk is treating DNA like a sequence, the same way we treat text or images in AI — going from next-token prediction on text to next-nucleotide prediction on the genome. Keep that sentence in your head, because by the end of the talk you'll fully understand what it means. Quick note before we start: this talk assumes you already know AI basics, like what a transformer is, what attention is, and what a foundation model is — that's a big model trained once on a lot of data, which can then be used for many different jobs without retraining from scratch. What you probably don't know is biology, and that's totally fine. I'll explain every biology term the moment it shows up, in plain words. Slide 2: The Evolution of Foundation Models To answer that, it helps to walk through how AI got here in the first place. In the early days, AI was task-specific. That means one model did one job. Let's start with BRCA1 mutation classification, scored using something called AUROC — a common way of scoring how well a model can tell two groups apart, in this case harmful mutations versus harmless ones, in the BRCA1 gene, which, as I mentioned, is closely linked to breast and ovarian cancer risk. The score goes from 0.5, meaning the model is basically just guessing randomly, up to 1.0, meaning it separates the two groups perfectly. Evo 2, with absolutely no extra training, just using its own built-in sense of what normal DNA looks like, scores 0.95 at telling apart harmful from harmless changes in BRCA1. That's a genuinely strong score for a model that was never specifically trained for this exact task. Adding a small, extra classifier trained on top of Evo 2's internal understanding gets roughly the same score on this particular test. And later follow-up research, training a similar small classifier across a much bigger set of about 830,000 known DNA changes, pushed the score up to 0.997 — showing that with more labeled examples to learn from, you can push performance even higher, and it also works well, without extra training, on insertions and deletions, types of changes it wasn't specifically trained to handle. Beyond that one gene, Evo 2 leads other similar methods specifically at judging mutations outside actual gene regions — remember, this is historically the hardest type to figure out, so doing well here really means something. Maybe the most interesting result in the whole talk is what researchers found when they looked inside Evo 2's internal workings, using special tools built for understanding what's going on inside a model. They found it had quietly learned to represent things like the boundaries between coding and non-coding parts of a gene, spots where proteins that control genes attach to DNA, and even pieces of protein structure. Nobody ever told the model to look for any of this. It just showed up naturally as a side effect of trying to guess the next letter really well — and this is the exact same thing we've seen happen in language models, which pick up grammar and meaning just from trying to guess the next word. There's also a striking generalization test: Evo 2 was able to correctly label parts of the woolly mammoth genome, an extinct species, using only the raw DNA sequence, with zero training data specifically about mammoths. That's a real test of whether the model actually learned general biological rules, instead of just memorizing what it saw during training. Worth being honest here though: other researchers who tested Evo 2 independently found that its performance changes depending on the type of gene or mutation, which is a good reminder that one strong overall number doesn't always tell the whole story. That honest note is actually the perfect lead-in to where we look more carefully at where this model still has weaknesses.

Researchers can improve the accuracy further by adding a small classifier, called a probe, on top of the model. This method is especially useful for difficult mutations outside genes, for important genes like BRCA1, and it works across many different species because Evo 2 was trained on DNA from across the tree of life. Slide 11: Generating DNA: Biological Design Evo 2's second big skill flips the same mechanism around. Because it was trained to always guess the next letter, you can also just run it forward instead of only using it to score existing sequences. You start with some beginning sequence, or even nothing at all, and you pick one letter at a time based on what the model thinks is likely to come next. Then you feed that chosen letter back in as new context, and repeat the whole process again and again. This is exactly the same idea used to generate text with a chatbot — the only real difference is you're working with four possible letters instead of a huge vocabulary of words, and "making sense" here means looking like real, working DNA instead of a coherent sentence. According to the paper, sequences created this way make sense not just letter by letter, but across the whole sequence, at the scale of an entire genome. That means Evo 2 can generate DNA that looks like it could belong to real mitochondria — a small structure inside cells — real bacteria, and even more complex organisms, and by several measurements, these generated sequences look more natural and realistic than ones made by earlier methods. But just picking letters at random only gets you "some" believable sequence. For real design work, scientists usually want a sequence with a specific goal in mind, like a particular structure related to how DNA gets packaged and controlled inside a cell. That's where guided search comes in: instead of retraining the whole model for every new goal, you steer the letter-picking process itself while it's happening, checking and adjusting partial sequences as they're being built, to push them toward the property you actually want. If that reminds you of guided or constrained text generation in language models, where you steer the output toward a certain style or rule without retraining anything, that's exactly the same idea, just applied to DNA. The paper says this is the first time anyone has shown that spending more computer effort on this guided search, at the moment of generating, actually leads to better results in biology — which is similar to a trend you may have seen in language and reasoning AI models recently, where doing more "thinking" at answer time improves the output. So between this skill and the last one, you now have the full picture of what Evo 2 can do with one trained model: read DNA to predict how

Slide 3: Understanding DNA as Information Let's cover some quick biology, and I'll tie it straight back to AI ideas you already know. DNA is built from four basic building blocks, called bases: A, T, G, and C, standing for Adenine, Thymine, Guanine, and Cytosine. That's really it. That is the entire "alphabet" that all life is written in. A genome is just the full DNA sequence of a living thing. It's basically a very long string made only from these four letters — from a few million letters for a simple bacteria, to over three billion letters for a human. Here's the important part for this audience: one single DNA letter can be treated just like a token in a language model. If you remember, a token is just a small piece of text, like a word or part of a word, that a language model reads one at a time. In DNA, each letter is one token. Its meaning depends on the letters around it, and in theory, you could predict it just from its surroundings, the same way a language model predicts the next word in a sentence. A gene is a piece of the DNA sequence that actually does something useful, kind of like one meaningful sentence hiding inside a very long, mostly boring document. A mutation is just a small change to that string — one letter gets swapped, added, or removed. And just like changing one word in a contract can totally change its meaning, changing one DNA letter in the right spot can break how a gene works, while changing a letter in another spot might do almost nothing. This is really the whole point I want you to take from this: order matters, just like word order matters in a sentence; one small change can flip the meaning completely, just like a typo can change what a sentence means; and sequence models — transformers, Hyena, or older models like RNNs — were built exactly to handle this kind of problem, predicting one symbol from the symbols around it. So the reason we can even try to use AI sequence models on DNA comes down to this: DNA is a string of symbols where order matters and small changes matter a lot, and that is exactly the kind of problem modern AI models are good at solving. Now that we've covered that, let's talk about why this approach is needed right now, more than ever before. Slide 4: Why Biology Needs Foundation Models The timing for a model like Evo 2 is not a coincidence. The cost of reading out DNA has dropped about ten thousand times since 2007. In simple terms, it used to be very expensive to read someone's or something's DNA, and now it's incredibly cheap. Because of that, we now have a flood of raw DNA data sitting in public databases — way more than any group of scientists could ever go through and label by hand, one piece

two things: it predicts variant effects, and it generates new DNA. Those are the two big things Evo 2 can do, and we'll spend a full slide on each one later. One more important point: the same trained model, with no extra training needed, is used both for guessing outcomes with zero-shot prediction — meaning it can do the task without ever being specifically trained on it — and for creating new sequences one letter at a time. And the whole thing was released fully in the open: the model, the code, and the data. That matters a lot, because it's part of why other researchers were already able to test it, poke at it, and build follow-up work on it so quickly.

Slide 13: Limitations No model is perfect, and Evo 2 has some important limitations. First, everything it produces—whether it's a harmfulness score or a newly generated DNA sequence—is only a prediction, not a medical decision. Any result that could affect patient care must still be tested in a laboratory or confirmed through clinical studies before anyone acts on it. Second, because Evo 2 can generate realistic DNA sequences, there's a genuine concern about misuse. The same technology that can be used for helpful applications in synthetic biology could also be misused. To reduce this risk, the researchers excluded viruses that infect plants, animals, and humans from the training data, making it harder for the model to help generate something dangerous. This is an important safety measure, but it doesn't eliminate all the risks, especially since the model is fully open. Another limitation is the amount of computing power needed to train a model like this. Training required over 1,000 GPUs and trillions of DNA letters, making it unrealistic for most universities or research labs to build a similar model from scratch. Finally, Evo 2 doesn't perform equally well on every type of gene or mutation. Independent studies found that its accuracy varies depending on the task, and some datasets contain far more harmless mutations than harmful ones, which can make the overall score look better than the model's performance on the rarer, more important cases. This reminds us that we should always look beyond a single accuracy score when evaluating an AI model. Now that we've covered both the strengths and limitations, let's look at where this research could go in the future. Slide 14: Future Directions The paper also discusses where models like Evo 2 could be useful in the future. In drug discovery, it can help researchers identify which mutations are worth testing, saving time and money. Because DNA contains the instructions for making proteins, Evo 2 could also support protein engineering by helping design DNA that produces proteins with useful properties. In synthetic biology, future versions may even help design entire genomes instead of just small DNA sequences. Another exciting application is personalized medicine, where the model could predict whether a person's unique genetic variants are likely to be harmful. Beyond biology, the StripedHyena 2 architecture could also benefit AI systems that need to process very long sequences, such as long documents, codebases, or videos. Looking further ahead, researchers also hope to build models that learn from DNA, RNA, and proteins together for a more complete understanding of biology

Now let's go one level deeper and understand how a model like this actually learns to do any of that, when nobody hand-labels DNA data with the "right answers." Slide 6: How Evo 2 Learns The training process works in a few simple steps. You start with a raw DNA sequence, just a long string like "...ATCGGCTA..." That string gets broken into tokens, one letter at a time. Remember, a token is just one small piece the model reads at a time. Unlike some language models, which group several letters together into one token, here every single DNA letter gets its own token — nothing gets squeezed together or simplified. The model then predicts the next letter, and that prediction gets compared to what the real next letter actually was, using something called cross-entropy loss, which is just a math way of measuring how wrong or right a guess was — it's the exact same method used to train language models. This process repeats at every single position in the genome, over and over, trillions of times, and the model is never told what a gene is or what a mutation is. It only ever tries to guess the next letter. Why does this actually work? First, no labels are needed. The correct answer here is simply whatever letter actually comes next in a real DNA sequence — and that's available in unlimited amounts, with zero human work needed to label it. Compare that to trying to build a list of "these mutations are harmful, these are not" by hand, which would take forever. Second, this forces the model to learn useful patterns along the way. DNA is built from four basic building blocks, called bases: A, T, G, and C, standing for Adenine, Thymine, Guanine, and Cytosine. That's really it. That is the entire "alphabet" that all life is written in. A genome is just the full DNA sequence of a living thing. It's basically a very long string made only from these four letters — from a few million letters for a simple bacteria, to over three billion letters for a human. Here's the important part for this audience: one single DNA letter can be treated just like a token in a language model. If you remember, a token is just a small piece of text, like a word or part of a word, that a language model reads one at a time. In DNA, each letter is one token. Its meaning depends on the letters around it, and in theory, you could predict it just from its surroundings, the same way a language model predicts the next word in a sentence. A gene is a piece of the DNA sequence that actually does something useful, kind of like one meaningful sentence hiding inside a very long, mostly boring document. A mutation is just a small change to that string — one letter gets swapped, added, or removed. And just like changing one word in a contract can totally change its meaning, changing one DNA letter in the right spot can break how a gene works, while changing a letter in another spot might do almost nothing. This is really the whole point I want you to take from this: order matters, just like word order matters in a sentence; one small change can flip the meaning completely, just like a typo can change what a sentence means; and sequence models — transformers, Hyena, or older models like RNNs — were built exactly to handle this kind of problem, predicting one symbol from the symbols around it. So the reason we can even try to use AI sequence models on DNA comes down to this: DNA is a string of symbols where order matters and small changes matter a lot, and that is exactly the kind of problem modern AI models are good at solving. First, everything it produces—whether it's a harmfulness score or a newly generated DNA sequence—is only a prediction, not a medical decision. Second, because Evo 2 can generate realistic DNA sequences, there's a genuine concern about misuse. The same technology that can be used for helpful applications in synthetic biology could also be misused. To reduce this risk, the researchers excluded viruses that infect plants, animals, and humans from the training data, making it harder for the model to help generate something dangerous. This is an important safety measure, but it doesn't eliminate all the risks, especially since the model is fully open. Another limitation is the amount of computing power needed to train a model like this. Training required over 1,000 GPUs and trillions of DNA letters, making it unrealistic for most universities or research labs to build a similar model from scratch. Finally, Evo 2 doesn't perform equally well on every type of gene or mutation. Independent studies found that its accuracy varies depending on the task, and some datasets contain far more harmless mutations than harmful ones, which can make the overall score look better than the model's performance on the rarer, more important cases. This reminds us that we should always look beyond a single accuracy score when evaluating an AI model. First, everything it produces—whether it's a harmfulness score or a newly generated DNA sequence—is only a prediction, not a medical decision. Any result that could affect patient care must still be tested in a laboratory or confirmed through clinical studies before anyone acts on it. Second, because Evo 2 can generate realistic DNA sequences, there's a genuine concern about misuse. The same technology that can be used for helpful applications in synthetic biology could also be misused. To reduce this risk, the researchers excluded viruses that infect plants, animals, and humans from the training data, making it harder for the model to help generate something dangerous. This is an important safety measure, but it doesn't eliminate all the risks, especially since the model is fully open. Another limitation is the amount of computing power needed to train a model like this. Training required over 1,000 GPUs and trillions of DNA letters, making it unrealistic for most universities or research labs to build a similar model from scratch. Finally, Evo 2 doesn't perform equally well on every type of gene or mutation. Independent studies found that its accuracy varies depending on the task, and some datasets contain far more harmless mutations than harmful ones, which can make the overall score look better than the model's performance on the rarer, more important cases. This reminds us that we should always look beyond a single accuracy score when evaluating an AI model. Now that we've covered both the strengths and limitations, let's look at where this research could go in the future. Standard attention, the method used in regular transformers, works by comparing every single position in a sequence to every other position. That means if you double how long your sequence is, the amount of computer work goes up by four times, not two times — that's what's called quadratic growth, versus the much gentler, near-linear growth we want instead. That's fine for the sequence lengths normal language models deal with, usually a few thousand up to maybe a hundred thousand tokens. But it becomes completely unworkable once you're talking about a million tokens, especially when you're training a huge model on trillions of examples. Scope The system will cover scheduled lead collection from online platforms, recency filtering, lead management, AI-based scoring with optional manual verification, personalized email outreach and engagement tracking, voice-based client interaction, requirement extraction, meeting scheduling and follow-up management. It will provide a web-based dashboard for reviewing leads, conversations, projects and their status with scheduled meetings added to the calendar. The system will assist human representatives rather than independently finalize or acquire projects. 5. Proposed Methodology Following an incremental software development approach, the system will be developed and integrated in successive stages. Initially, a scheduler will periodically trigger the lead-generation module to collect potential leads from selected online platforms. The collected data will undergo preprocessing, recency filtering and lead management to remove outdated or duplicate entries. In the next stage, leads will undergo AI-based scoring and qualification, with an option for manual verification to identify relevant and genuine leads. Qualified leads will then be contacted through personalized email outreach with engagement and responses tracked by the system. For leads requiring phone interaction, a voice-based conversational agent will be implemented by integrating speech-to-text, an LLM for processing customer responses and generating text responses and text-to-speech for converting the generated responses into speech. Relevant project requirements will be extracted and summarized from client interactions. Finally, the system will provide meeting scheduling and calendar integration, along with a centralized web-based dashboard for managing leads, communications, conversations, projects, meetings and their status. Each module will be tested incrementally before being integrated into the complete system. Reference: The project is inspired by Apollo.io’s lead generation and outreach capabilities, while extending the workflow with a voice agent that communicates with potential leads and automatically extracts and summarizes their project requirements.

It came out in the journal Nature in 2026, and the title is "Genome modelling and design across all domains of life with Evo 2." It was made by a big team, led by the Arc Institute and NVIDIA, along with Stanford, UCSF, Berkeley, and a few other groups. The main idea behind this whole talk is treating DNA like a sequence, the same way we treat text or images in AI — going from next-token prediction on text to next-nucleotide prediction on the genome. Keep that sentence in your head, because by the end of the talk you'll fully understand what it means. Quick note before we start: this talk assumes you already know AI basics, like what a transformer is, what attention is, and what a foundation model is — that's a big model trained once on a lot of data, which can then be used for many different jobs without retraining from scratch. What you probably don't know is biology, and that's totally fine. I'll explain every biology term the moment it shows up, in plain words. Let's start with a simple question: how did we even get to the point where someone would try to build "GPT, but for the genome"? Slide 2: The Evolution of Foundation Models To answer that, it helps to walk through how AI got here in the first place. In the early days, AI was task-specific. That means one model did one job. You'd build a separate model for spotting spam, another one for translating language, another one for recognizing pictures. Each of these needed its own labeled data, made carefully by hand. Then GPT changed the game. Instead of building a new model for every job, you train one big model with a very simple goal: guess the next word. You train it on huge amounts of raw text that nobody had to label by hand, and that one model turns out to be useful for many different tasks afterward, without needing to be rebuilt each time. Vision models did something similar with images, learning straight from raw pixels. Then multimodal models combined text, images, and audio into one shared model. Notice the pattern here: at each step, the model gets more general, the training data gets less carefully labeled, and the model has to figure out more on its own. So here's the big question this whole progression is building toward: if this idea worked for text, then for images, then for many types of data together, could it also work on something no human ever wrote — the code that nature itself has been writing for four billion years through evolution? retrieval_candidates.document: Slide 13: Limitations No model is perfect, and Evo 2 has some important limitations. First, everything it produces—whether it's a harmfulness score or a newly generated DNA sequence—is only a prediction, not a medical decision. Any result that could affect patient care must still be tested in a laboratory or confirmed through clinical studies before anyone acts on it. Second, because Evo 2 can generate realistic DNA sequences, there's a genuine concern about misuse. The same technology that can be used for helpful applications in synthetic biology could also be misused. To reduce this risk, the researchers excluded viruses that infect plants, animals, and humans from the training data, making it harder for the model to help generate something dangerous. This is an important safety measure, but it doesn't eliminate all the risks, especially since the model is fully open. Another limitation is the amount of computing power needed to train a model like this. Training required over 1,000 GPUs and trillions of DNA letters, making it unrealistic for most universities or research labs to build a similar model from scratch. Finally, Evo 2 doesn't perform equally well on every type of gene or mutation. Independent studies found that its accuracy varies depending on the task, and some datasets contain far more harmless mutations than harmful ones, which can make the overall score look better than the model's performance on the rarer, more important cases. This reminds us that we should always look beyond a single accuracy score when evaluating an AI model. Now that we've covered both the strengths and limitations, let's look at where this research could go in the future. Slide 14: Future Directions The paper also discusses where models like Evo 2 could be useful in the future. In drug discovery, it can help researchers identify which mutations are worth testing, saving time and money. Because DNA contains the instructions for making proteins, Evo 2 could also support protein engineering by helping design DNA that produces proteins with useful properties. In synthetic biology, future versions may even help design entire genomes instead of just small DNA sequences. Another exciting application is personalized medicine, where the model could predict whether a person's unique genetic variants are likely to be harmful. Beyond biology, the StripedHyena 2 architecture could also benefit AI systems that need to process very long sequences, such as long documents, codebases, or videos. Looking further ahead, researchers also hope to build models that learn from DNA, RNA, and proteins together for a more complete understanding of biology

retrieval_candidates.document: Slide 3: Understanding DNA as Information Let's cover some quick biology, and I'll tie it straight back to AI ideas you already know. DNA is built from four basic building blocks, called bases: A, T, G, and C, standing for Adenine, Thymine, Guanine, and Cytosine. That's really it. That is the entire "alphabet" that all life is written in. A genome is just the full DNA sequence of a living thing. It's basically a very long string made only from these four letters — from a few million letters for a simple bacteria, to over three billion letters for a human. Here's the important part for this audience: one single DNA letter can be treated just like a token in a language model. If you remember, a token is just a small piece of text, like a word or part of a word, that a language model reads one at a time. In DNA, each letter is one token. Its meaning depends on the letters around it, and in theory, you could predict it just from its surroundings, the same way a language model predicts the next word in a sentence. A gene is a piece of the DNA sequence that actually does something useful, kind of like one meaningful sentence hiding inside a very long, mostly boring document. A mutation is just a small change to that string — one letter gets swapped, added, or removed. And just like changing one word in a contract can totally change its meaning, changing one DNA letter in the right spot can break how a gene works, while changing a letter in another spot might do almost nothing. This is really the whole point I want you to take from this: order matters, just like word order matters in a sentence; one small change can flip the meaning completely, just like a typo can change what a sentence means; and sequence models — transformers, Hyena, or older models like RNNs — were built exactly to handle this kind of problem, predicting one symbol from the symbols around it. So the reason we can even try to use AI sequence models on DNA comes down to this: DNA is a string of symbols where order matters and small changes matter a lot, and that is exactly the kind of problem modern AI models are good at solving. Now that we've covered that, let's talk about why this approach is needed right now, more than ever before. Let's start with BRCA1 mutation classification, scored using something called AUROC — a common way of scoring how well a model can tell two groups apart, in this case harmful mutations versus harmless ones, in the BRCA1 gene, which, as I mentioned, is closely linked to breast and ovarian cancer risk. The score goes from 0.5, meaning the model is basically just guessing randomly, up to 1.0, meaning it separates the two groups perfectly. Evo 2, with absolutely no extra training, just using its own built-in sense of what normal DNA looks like, scores 0.95 at telling apart harmful from harmless changes in BRCA1. That's a genuinely strong score for a model that was never specifically trained for this exact task. Adding a small, extra classifier trained on top of Evo 2's internal understanding gets roughly the same score on this particular test. And later follow-up research, training a similar small classifier across a much bigger set of about 830,000 known DNA changes, pushed the score up to 0.997 — showing that with more labeled examples to learn from, you can push performance even higher, and it also works well, without extra training, on insertions and deletions, types of changes it wasn't specifically trained to handle. Beyond that one gene, Evo 2 leads other similar methods specifically at judging mutations outside actual gene regions — remember, this is historically the hardest type to figure out, so doing well here really means something. Maybe the most interesting result in the whole talk is what researchers found when they looked inside Evo 2's internal workings, using special tools built for understanding what's going on inside a model. They found it had quietly learned to represent things like the boundaries between coding and non-coding parts of a gene, spots where proteins that control genes attach to DNA, and even pieces of protein structure. Nobody ever told the model to look for any of this. It just showed up naturally as a side effect of trying to guess the next letter really well — and this is the exact same thing we've seen happen in language models, which pick up grammar and meaning just from trying to guess the next word. There's also a striking generalization test: Evo 2 was able to correctly label parts of the woolly mammoth genome, an extinct species, using only the raw DNA sequence, with zero training data specifically about mammoths. That's a real test of whether the model actually learned general biological rules, instead of just memorizing what it saw during training. Worth being honest here though: other researchers who tested Evo 2 independently found that its performance changes depending on the type of gene or mutation, which is a good reminder that one strong overall number doesn't always tell the whole story. That honest note is actually the perfect lead-in to where we look more carefully at where this model still has weaknesses.

So if you want to catch these long-distance relationships, you genuinely need a model that can look across that much space at once — you can't just fake it with a clever shortcut. The proposed system aims to automate these activities through scheduled lead collection, lead filtering, AI-based scoring and personalized outreach. Qualified leads will be contacted via email while a voice-based conversational agent will handle phone interactions and assist in understanding their requirements. The system will centralize leads, communications and projects through a web-based dashboard enabling efficient human follow-up. 3. Objectives -Development of an automated system for scheduled collection and management of potential project leads. -Implementation of lead filtering, AI-based scoring and optional manual verification for lead qualification. -Generation of personalized client outreach based on available lead information by implementing email-based client communication & engagement tracking and developing a voice-based conversational agent using speech processing and an LLM for client interaction. -Extraction and summarization of project requirements from client conversations. -Provision of a centralized dashboard for managing leads, communication, projects and human follow-up.

Initially, a scheduler will periodically trigger the lead-generation module to collect potential leads from selected online platforms. The collected data will undergo preprocessing, recency filtering and lead management to remove outdated or duplicate entries. In the next stage, leads will undergo AI-based scoring and qualification, with an option for manual verification to identify relevant and genuine leads. Qualified leads will then be contacted through personalized email outreach with engagement and responses tracked by the system. For leads requiring phone interaction, a voice-based conversational agent will be implemented by integrating speech-to-text, an LLM for processing customer responses and generating text responses and text-to-speech for converting the generated responses into speech. Relevant project requirements will be extracted and summarized from client interactions. Finally, the system will provide meeting scheduling and calendar integration, along with a centralized web-based dashboard for managing leads, communications, conversations, projects, meetings and their status. Each module will be tested incrementally before being integrated into the complete system. Now let's go one level deeper and understand how a model like this actually learns to do any of that, when nobody hand-labels DNA data with the "right answers." Slide 6: How Evo 2 Learns The training process works in a few simple steps. You start with a raw DNA sequence, just a long string like "...ATCGGCTA..." That string gets broken into tokens, one letter at a time. Remember, a token is just one small piece the model reads at a time. Unlike some language models, which group several letters together into one token, here every single DNA letter gets its own token — nothing gets squeezed together or simplified. The model then predicts the next letter, and that prediction gets compared to what the real next letter actually was, using something called cross-entropy loss, which is just a math way of measuring how wrong or right a guess was — it's the exact same method used to train language models. This process repeats at every single position in the genome, over and over, trillions of times, and the model is never told what a gene is or what a mutation is. It only ever tries to guess the next letter. Why does this actually work? First, no labels are needed. The correct answer here is simply whatever letter actually comes next in a real DNA sequence — and that's available in unlimited amounts, with zero human work needed to label it. Compare that to trying to build a list of "these mutations are harmful, these are not" by hand, which would take forever. Second, this forces the model to learn useful patterns along the way. To get good at guessing the next letter, the model is forced to quietly pick up real structure — things like codons, which are little three-letter groups that spell out instructions for building proteins, common patterns called motifs, and the "grammar" of how genes are controlled — even though nobody ever directly taught it any of these ideas. And third, this is basically the exact same method used to train large language models: try to guess what comes next, given everything before it. So here's what I want you to remember: Evo 2's training method didn't need any special biology knowledge to design. It's the same self-supervised method used everywhere else in AI, just pointed at a four- letter alphabet instead of a huge vocabulary of words. This brings up an obvious engineering problem though. retrieval_candidates.document: Slide 12: Experimental Results Now for real, measured numbers. Let's start with BRCA1 mutation classification, scored using something called AUROC — a common way of scoring how well a model can tell two groups apart, in this case harmful mutations versus harmless ones, in the BRCA1 gene, which, as I mentioned, is closely linked to breast and ovarian cancer risk. The score goes from 0.5, meaning the model is basically just guessing randomly, up to 1.0, meaning it separates the two groups perfectly. Evo 2, with absolutely no extra training, just using its own built-in sense of what normal DNA looks like, scores 0.95 at telling apart harmful from harmless changes in BRCA1. That's a genuinely strong score for a model that was never specifically trained for this exact task. Adding a small, extra classifier trained on top of Evo 2's internal understanding gets roughly the same score on this particular test. And later follow-up research, training a similar small classifier across a much bigger set of about 830,000 known DNA changes, pushed the score up to 0.997 — showing that with more labeled examples to learn from, you can push performance even higher, and it also works well, without extra training, on insertions and deletions, types of changes it wasn't specifically trained to handle. Beyond that one gene, Evo 2 leads other similar methods specifically at judging mutations outside actual gene regions — remember, this is historically the hardest type to figure out, so doing well here really means something. Maybe the most interesting result in the whole talk is what researchers found when they looked inside Evo 2's internal workings, using special tools built for understanding what's going on inside a model. They found it had quietly learned to represent things like the boundaries between coding and non-coding parts of a gene, spots where proteins that control genes attach to DNA, and even pieces of protein structure. Nobody ever told the model to look for any of this. It just showed up naturally as a side effect of trying to guess the next letter really well — and this is the exact same thing we've seen happen in language models, which pick up grammar and meaning just from trying to guess the next word. There's also a striking generalization test: Evo 2 was able to correctly label parts of the woolly mammoth genome, an extinct species, using only the raw DNA sequence, with zero training data specifically about mammoths. That's a real test of whether the model actually learned general biological rules, instead of just memorizing what it saw during training. Worth being honest here though: other researchers who tested Evo 2 independently found that its performance changes depending on the type of gene or mutation, which is a good reminder that one strong overall number doesn't always tell the whole story. That honest note is actually the perfect lead-in to where we look more carefully at where this model still has weaknesses.

retrieval_candidates.document: Slide 13: Limitations No model is perfect, and Evo 2 has some important limitations. First, everything it produces—whether it's a harmfulness score or a newly generated DNA sequence—is only a prediction, not a medical decision. Any result that could affect patient care must still be tested in a laboratory or confirmed through clinical studies before anyone acts on it. Second, because Evo 2 can generate realistic DNA sequences, there's a genuine concern about misuse. The same technology that can be used for helpful applications in synthetic biology could also be misused. To reduce this risk, the researchers excluded viruses that infect plants, animals, and humans from the training data, making it harder for the model to help generate something dangerous. This is an important safety measure, but it doesn't eliminate all the risks, especially since the model is fully open. Another limitation is the amount of computing power needed to train a model like this. DNA is built from four basic building blocks, called bases: A, T, G, and C, standing for Adenine, Thymine, Guanine, and Cytosine. That's really it. That is the entire "alphabet" that all life is written in. A genome is just the full DNA sequence of a living thing. It's basically a very long string made only from these four letters — from a few million letters for a simple bacteria, to over three billion letters for a human. Here's the important part for this audience: one single DNA letter can be treated just like a token in a language model. If you remember, a token is just a small piece of text, like a word or part of a word, that a language model reads one at a time. In DNA, each letter is one token. Its meaning depends on the letters around it, and in theory, you could predict it just from its surroundings, the same way a language model predicts the next word in a sentence. A gene is a piece of the DNA sequence that actually does something useful, kind of like one meaningful sentence hiding inside a very long, mostly boring document. A mutation is just a small change to that string — one letter gets swapped, added, or removed. And just like changing one word in a contract can totally change its meaning, changing one DNA letter in the right spot can break how a gene works, while changing a letter in another spot might do almost nothing. This is really the whole point I want you to take from this: order matters, just like word order matters in a sentence; one small change can flip the meaning completely, just like a typo can change what a sentence means; and sequence models — transformers, Hyena, or older models like RNNs — were built exactly to handle this kind of problem, predicting one symbol from the symbols around it. So the reason we can even try to use AI sequence models on DNA comes down to this: DNA is a string of symbols where order matters and small changes matter a lot, and that is exactly the kind of problem modern AI models are good at solving. Now let's go one level deeper and understand how a model like this actually learns to do any of that, when nobody hand-labels DNA data with the "right answers." Slide 6: How Evo 2 Learns The training process works in a few simple steps. You start with a raw DNA sequence, just a long string like "...ATCGGCTA..." That string gets broken into tokens, one letter at a time. Remember, a token is just one small piece the model reads at a time. Unlike some language models, which group several letters together into one token, here every single DNA letter gets its own token — nothing gets squeezed together or simplified. The model then predicts the next letter, and that prediction gets compared to what the real next letter actually was, using something called cross-entropy loss, which is just a math way of measuring how wrong or right a guess was — it's the exact same method used to train language models. This process repeats at every single position in the genome, over and over, trillions of times, and the model is never told what a gene is or what a mutation is. It only ever tries to guess the next letter. Why does this actually work? First, no labels are needed. The correct answer here is simply whatever letter actually comes next in a real DNA sequence — and that's available in unlimited amounts, with zero human work needed to label it. Compare that to trying to build a list of "these mutations are harmful, these are not" by hand, which would take forever. Second, this forces the model to learn useful patterns along the way. To get good at guessing the next letter, the model is forced to quietly pick up real structure — things like codons, which are little three-letter groups that spell out instructions for building proteins, common patterns called motifs, and the "grammar" of how genes are controlled — even though nobody ever directly taught it any of these ideas. And third, this is basically the exact same method used to train large language models: try to guess what comes next, given everything before it. So here's what I want you to remember: Evo 2's training method didn't need any special biology knowledge to design. It's the same self-supervised method used everywhere else in AI, just pointed at a four- letter alphabet instead of a huge vocabulary of words. This brings up an obvious engineering problem though. This is one single trained model, used without any extra training, for both prediction and generation, across every branch of life — not a bunch of separate specialized models. It runs on an architecture that actually scales: StripedHyena 2 is the reason a million-letter view at full detail is even possible, something a regular transformer just couldn't manage. It was also released fully open — the trained model, the code, and the entire 9.3 trillion letter OpenGenome2 dataset were all made freely available, which is a big part of why so much follow-up research already exists on this model in such a short time. And maybe most interesting of all, the model figured out real biology on its own: patterns like gene boundaries and control switches showed up on their own, with zero labels involved, purely as a side effect of the model trying to guess the next DNA letter — the exact same thing we've seen happen again and again with language models, just now shown in a completely different area, biology. I want to leave you with this thought: if GPT learned the language written by people, Evo 2 is learning the language written by four billion years of evolution. I want to be clear that this isn't a settled fact — it's really an open question the field is still working through. Whether genomic models will actually keep improving the same way language models have, and how far this comparison really holds up, is something researchers are still actively figuring out.

Slide 12: Experimental Results Now for real, measured numbers. Let's start with BRCA1 mutation classification, scored using something called AUROC — a common way of scoring how well a model can tell two groups apart, in this case harmful mutations versus harmless ones, in the BRCA1 gene, which, as I mentioned, is closely linked to breast and ovarian cancer risk. The score goes from 0.5, meaning the model is basically just guessing randomly, up to 1.0, meaning it separates the two groups perfectly. That's a genuinely strong score for a model that was never specifically trained for this exact task. Maybe the most interesting result in the whole talk is what researchers found when they looked inside Evo 2's internal workings, using special tools built for understanding what's going on inside a model. They found it had quietly learned to represent things like the boundaries between coding and non-coding parts of a gene, spots where proteins that control genes attach to DNA, and even pieces of protein structure. Nobody ever told the model to look for any of this. It just showed up naturally as a side effect of trying to guess the next letter really well — and this is the exact same thing we've seen happen in language models, which pick up grammar and meaning just from trying to guess the next word. There's also a striking generalization test: Evo 2 was able to correctly label parts of the woolly mammoth genome, an extinct species, using only the raw DNA sequence, with zero training data specifically about mammoths. That's a real test of whether the model actually learned general biological rules, instead of just memorizing what it saw during training. And maybe most interesting of all, the model figured out real biology on its own: patterns like gene boundaries and control switches showed up on their own, with zero labels involved, purely as a side effect of the model trying to guess the next DNA letter — the exact same thing we've seen happen again and again with language models, just now shown in a completely different area, biology. I want to leave you with this thought: if GPT learned the language written by people, Evo 2 is learning the language written by four billion years of evolution. I want to be clear that this isn't a settled fact — it's really an open question the field is still working through. It came out in the journal Nature in 2026, and the title is "Genome modelling and design across all domains of life with Evo 2." It was made by a big team, led by the Arc Institute and NVIDIA, along with Stanford, UCSF, Berkeley, and a few other groups. The main idea behind this whole talk is treating DNA like a sequence, the same way we treat text or images in AI — going from next-token prediction on text to next-nucleotide prediction on the genome. Keep that sentence in your head, because by the end of the talk you'll fully understand what it means. Quick note before we start: this talk assumes you already know AI basics, like what a transformer is, what attention is, and what a foundation model is — that's a big model trained once on a lot of data, which can then be used for many different jobs without retraining from scratch. What you probably don't know is biology, and that's totally fine. I'll explain every biology term the moment it shows up, in plain words. Let's start with a simple question: how did we even get to the point where someone would try to build "GPT, but for the genome"? Slide 2: The Evolution of Foundation Models To answer that, it helps to walk through how AI got here in the first place. In the early days, AI was task-specific. That means one model did one job. You'd build a separate model for spotting spam, another one for translating language, another one for recognizing pictures. Each of these needed its own labeled data, made carefully by hand. Then GPT changed the game. Instead of building a new model for every job, you train one big model with a very simple goal: guess the next word. You train it on huge amounts of raw text that nobody had to label by hand, and that one model turns out to be useful for many different tasks afterward, without needing to be rebuilt each time. Vision models did something similar with images, learning straight from raw pixels. Then multimodal models combined text, images, and audio into one shared model. Notice the pattern here: at each step, the model gets more general, the training data gets less carefully labeled, and the model has to figure out more on its own. So here's the big question this whole progression is building toward: if this idea worked for text, then for images, then for many types of data together, could it also work on something no human ever wrote — the code that nature itself has been writing for four billion years through evolution? Let's start with BRCA1 mutation classification, scored using something called AUROC — a common way of scoring how well a model can tell two groups apart, in this case harmful mutations versus harmless ones, in the BRCA1 gene, which, as I mentioned, is closely linked to breast and ovarian cancer risk. The score goes from 0.5, meaning the model is basically just guessing randomly, up to 1.0, meaning it separates the two groups perfectly. Evo 2, with absolutely no extra training, just using its own built-in sense of what normal DNA looks like, scores 0.95 at telling apart harmful from harmless changes in BRCA1. That's a genuinely strong score for a model that was never specifically trained for this exact task. Adding a small, extra classifier trained on top of Evo 2's internal understanding gets roughly the same score on this particular test. And later follow-up research, training a similar small classifier across a much bigger set of about 830,000 known DNA changes, pushed the score up to 0.997 — showing that with more labeled examples to learn from, you can push performance even higher, and it also works well, without extra training, on insertions and deletions, types of changes it wasn't specifically trained to handle. Beyond that one gene, Evo 2 leads other similar methods specifically at judging mutations outside actual gene regions — remember, this is historically the hardest type to figure out, so doing well here really means something. Maybe the most interesting result in the whole talk is what researchers found when they looked inside Evo 2's internal workings, using special tools built for understanding what's going on inside a model. They found it had quietly learned to represent things like the boundaries between coding and non-coding parts of a gene, spots where proteins that control genes attach to DNA, and even pieces of protein structure. Slide 6: How Evo 2 Learns The training process works in a few simple steps. You start with a raw DNA sequence, just a long string like "...ATCGGCTA..." That string gets broken into tokens, one letter at a time. Remember, a token is just one small piece the model reads at a time. Unlike some language models, which group several letters together into one token, here every single DNA letter gets its own token — nothing gets squeezed together or simplified. The model then predicts the next letter, and that prediction gets compared to what the real next letter actually was, using something called cross-entropy loss, which is just a math way of measuring how wrong or right a guess was — it's the exact same method used to train language models. This process repeats at every single position in the genome, over and over, trillions of times, and the model is never told what a gene is or what a mutation is. It only ever tries to guess the next letter. Why does this actually work? First, no labels are needed. The correct answer here is simply whatever letter actually comes next in a real DNA sequence — and that's available in unlimited amounts, with zero human work needed to label it. Compare that to trying to build a list of "these mutations are harmful, these are not" by hand, which would take forever. Second, this forces the model to learn useful patterns along the way. To get good at guessing the next letter, the model is forced to quietly pick up real structure — things like codons, which are little three-letter groups that spell out instructions for building proteins, common patterns called motifs, and the "grammar" of how genes are controlled — even though nobody ever directly taught it any of these ideas. And third, this is basically the exact same method used to train large language models: try to guess what comes next, given everything before it. So here's what I want you to remember: Evo 2's training method didn't need any special biology knowledge to design. It's the same self-supervised method used everywhere else in AI, just pointed at a four- letter alphabet instead of a huge vocabulary of words. This brings up an obvious engineering problem though. retrieval_candidates.document: Slide 13: Limitations No model is perfect, and Evo 2 has some important limitations. First, everything it produces—whether it's a harmfulness score or a newly generated DNA sequence—is only a prediction, not a medical decision. Any result that could affect patient care must still be tested in a laboratory or confirmed through clinical studies before anyone acts on it. Second, because Evo 2 can generate realistic DNA sequences, there's a genuine concern about misuse. The same technology that can be used for helpful applications in synthetic biology could also be misused. To reduce this risk, the researchers excluded viruses that infect plants, animals, and humans from the training data, making it harder for the model to help generate something dangerous. This is an important safety measure, but it doesn't eliminate all the risks, especially since the model is fully open. Another limitation is the amount of computing power needed to train a model like this. Training required over 1,000 GPUs and trillions of DNA letters, making it unrealistic for most universities or research labs to build a similar model from scratch. Finally, Evo 2 doesn't perform equally well on every type of gene or mutation. Independent studies found that its accuracy varies depending on the task, and some datasets contain far more harmless mutations than harmful ones, which can make the overall score look better than the model's performance on the rarer, more important cases. This reminds us that we should always look beyond a single accuracy score when evaluating an AI model. Now that we've covered both the strengths and limitations, let's look at where this research could go in the future. Slide 14: Future Directions The paper also discusses where models like Evo 2 could be useful in the future. In drug discovery, it can help researchers identify which mutations are worth testing, saving time and money. Because DNA contains the instructions for making proteins, Evo 2 could also support protein engineering by helping design DNA that produces proteins with useful properties. In synthetic biology, future versions may even help design entire genomes instead of just small DNA sequences. retrieval_candidates.document: Slide 3: Understanding DNA as Information Let's cover some quick biology, and I'll tie it straight back to AI ideas you already know. DNA is built from four basic building blocks, called bases: A, T, G, and C, standing for Adenine, Thymine, Guanine, and Cytosine. That's really it. That is the entire "alphabet" that all life is written in. A genome is just the full DNA sequence of a living thing. It's basically a very long string made only from these four letters — from a few million letters for a simple bacteria, to over three billion letters for a human. Here's the important part for this audience: one single DNA letter can be treated just like a token in a language model. If you remember, a token is just a small piece of text, like a word or part of a word, that a language model reads one at a time. In DNA, each letter is one token. Its meaning depends on the letters around it, and in theory, you could predict it just from its surroundings, the same way a language model predicts the next word in a sentence. A gene is a piece of the DNA sequence that actually does something useful, kind of like one meaningful sentence hiding inside a very long, mostly boring document. A mutation is just a small change to that string — one letter gets swapped, added, or removed. And just like changing one word in a contract can totally change its meaning, changing one DNA letter in the right spot can break how a gene works, while changing a letter in another spot might do almost nothing. This is really the whole point I want you to take from this: order matters, just like word order matters in a sentence; one small change can flip the meaning completely, just like a typo can change what a sentence means; and sequence models — transformers, Hyena, or older models like RNNs — were built exactly to handle this kind of problem, predicting one symbol from the symbols around it. So the reason we can even try to use AI sequence models on DNA comes down to this: DNA is a string of symbols where order matters and small changes matter a lot, and that is exactly the kind of problem modern AI models are good at solving. Now that we've covered that, let's talk about why this approach is needed right now, more than ever before. final_evidence.document: Slide 7: Why Standard Transformers Are Not Enough Here's where we hit a real technical problem. Standard attention, the method used in regular transformers, works by comparing every single position in a sequence to every other position. That means if you double how long your sequence is, the amount of computer work goes up by four times, not two times — that's what's called quadratic growth, versus the much gentler, near-linear growth we want instead. That's fine for the sequence lengths normal language models deal with, usually a few thousand up to maybe a hundred thousand tokens. But it becomes completely unworkable once you're talking about a million tokens, especially when you're training a huge model on trillions of examples. And this really matters in biology, because the parts of DNA that control genes, and the connections between genes, can be spread hundreds of thousands, even millions, of letters apart. So if you want to catch these long-distance relationships, you genuinely need a model that can look across that much space at once — you can't just fake it with a clever shortcut. Put those two facts together, and you get the conclusion: at the level of looking at every single DNA letter, with a goal of a 1 million letter view, regular attention is simply too expensive to train, no matter how much computer hardware you have. This is actually the same wall that a lot of AI researchers have been running into with long text sequences too, which is why people have already built things like sparse attention, other efficient attention tricks, and convolution-based models like the earlier version of Hyena. Evo 2 builds on that same line of work, but has to push it even further, because DNA doesn't give you an easy shortcut the way language does — you really do need to look at every single letter, one at a time. So here's the real question: can we build a model whose cost grows slowly and gently as the sequence gets longer, while still being able to catch those important long-distance patterns, the way attention can? That answer is the single most important idea in this whole talk, and it's what we're covering next. Slide 8: This is the most important part of the talk, so let's take our time. Evo 2 uses a hybrid design made up of four repeating components that are stacked together to build the full model. Three of these are called SE, MR, and LI, which are different types of Hyena operators, and the fourth is a small amount of regular attention. SE, or Short Explicit Hyena, handles patterns that are close together in the sequence, like the three-letter codons we talked about earlier. MR, or Medium Regularized Hyena, handles patterns that are a bit farther apart. LI, or Long Implicit Hyena, is responsible for finding patterns over very long distances. Instead of storing one large fixed filter, it creates the filter when it's needed. This helps it capture long-range

However, attention is still better when the model needs to focus on one very specific piece of information. So, Evo 2 combines both approaches: the Hyena operators do most of the work because they're much cheaper, while attention is used only where its precision is most useful. This is what makes it possible for Evo 2 to process sequences as long as one million DNA letters. In fact, when the 40-billion-parameter model was trained using 1,024 GPUs, it trained faster than both the previous version and a standard transformer. So the main takeaway is that StripedHyena 2 doesn't replace attention completely—it simply uses it much less often, allowing the model to handle very long DNA sequences efficiently without losing accuracy. Evo 2 was built in two sizes: 7 billion and 40 billion parameters, and the larger model was trained using 1,024 GPUs. The model can eventually process up to 1 million DNA letters at once, but it wasn't trained on sequences that long from the beginning. Instead, training happened in two stages. During the first stage, called pretraining, the model looked at shorter DNA sequences and mainly focused on the most important parts of the genome, such as genes and the regions that control them. This helped it learn the basic patterns without spending huge amounts of computing power. Once it had learned those basics, the second stage, called midtraining, gradually increased the sequence length until the model could process 1 million DNA letters at once. This allowed the model to learn relationships between DNA regions that are very far apart. So the main idea is that Evo 2 didn't start with the hardest task. It first learned from shorter, information-rich sequences and then gradually moved to much longer ones, making the training process more efficient and practical. Instead of hand-building features for every single new question, you train one model on raw data, using a general self-supervised goal — meaning the model creates its own training signal from the data itself, without needing human labels — and then you reuse what that model learned for many different questions later. This is exactly the same idea that made modern language AI work so well. Worth mentioning here: earlier genomic models existed before Evo 2, like DNABERT or an earlier version called Evo 1, but they were limited — usually to shorter sequences, or to just one type of organism, like bacteria only. Here's really the map for the rest of the talk: all domains of life feed into OpenGenome2, the training set, and that trains Evo 2, which runs on something called the StripedHyena 2 architecture — don't worry, we'll explain exactly what that means in a few slides. From there, the model does two things: it predicts variant effects, and it generates new DNA. Those are the two big things Evo 2 can do, and we'll spend a full slide on each one later. Researchers can improve the accuracy further by adding a small classifier, called a probe, on top of the model. This method is especially useful for difficult mutations outside genes, for important genes like BRCA1, and it works across many different species because Evo 2 was trained on DNA from across the tree of life. Slide 11: Generating DNA: Biological Design Evo 2's second big skill flips the same mechanism around. Because it was trained to always guess the next letter, you can also just run it forward instead of only using it to score existing sequences. You start with some beginning sequence, or even nothing at all, and you pick one letter at a time based on what the model thinks is likely to come next. Then you feed that chosen letter back in as new context, and repeat the whole process again and again. This is exactly the same idea used to generate text with a chatbot — the only real difference is you're working with four possible letters instead of a huge vocabulary of words, and "making sense" here means looking like real, working DNA instead of a coherent sentence. According to the paper, sequences created this way make sense not just letter by letter, but across the whole sequence, at the scale of an entire genome. That means Evo 2 can generate DNA that looks like it could belong to real mitochondria — a small structure inside cells — real bacteria, and even more complex organisms, and by several measurements, these generated sequences look more natural and realistic than ones made by earlier methods. But just picking letters at random only gets you "some" believable sequence. For real design work, scientists usually want a sequence with a specific goal in mind, like a particular structure related to how DNA gets packaged and controlled inside a cell. That's where guided search comes in: instead of retraining the whole model for every new goal, you steer the letter-picking process itself while it's happening, checking and adjusting partial sequences as they're being built, to push them toward the property you actually want. If that reminds you of guided or constrained text generation in language models, where you steer the output toward a certain style or rule without retraining anything, that's exactly the same idea, just applied to DNA. The paper says this is the first time anyone has shown that spending more computer effort on this guided search, at the moment of generating, actually leads to better results in biology — which is similar to a trend you may have seen in language and reasoning AI models recently, where doing more "thinking" at answer time improves the output. retrieval_candidates.document: Slide 13: Limitations No model is perfect, and Evo 2 has some important limitations. First, everything it produces—whether it's a harmfulness score or a newly generated DNA sequence—is only a prediction, not a medical decision. Second, because Evo 2 can generate realistic DNA sequences, there's a genuine concern about misuse. The same technology that can be used for helpful applications in synthetic biology could also be misused. To reduce this risk, the researchers excluded viruses that infect plants, animals, and humans from the training data, making it harder for the model to help generate something dangerous. DNA is built from four basic building blocks, called bases: A, T, G, and C, standing for Adenine, Thymine, Guanine, and Cytosine. That's really it. That is the entire "alphabet" that all life is written in. A genome is just the full DNA sequence of a living thing. It's basically a very long string made only from these four letters — from a few million letters for a simple bacteria, to over three billion letters for a human. A gene is a piece of the DNA sequence that actually does something useful, kind of like one meaningful sentence hiding inside a very long, mostly boring document. A mutation is just a small change to that string — one letter gets swapped, added, or removed. This is really the whole point I want you to take from this: order matters, just like word order matters in a sentence; one small change can flip the meaning completely, just like a typo can change what a sentence means; and sequence models — transformers, Hyena, or older models like RNNs — were built exactly to handle this kind of problem, predicting one symbol from the symbols around it. So the reason we can even try to use AI sequence models on DNA comes down to this: DNA is a string of symbols where order matters and small changes matter a lot, and that is exactly the kind of problem modern AI models are good at solving. First, everything it produces—whether it's a harmfulness score or a newly generated DNA sequence—is only a prediction, not a medical decision. Second, because Evo 2 can generate realistic DNA sequences, there's a genuine concern about misuse. The same technology that can be used for helpful applications in synthetic biology could also be misused. To reduce this risk, the researchers excluded viruses that infect plants, animals, and humans from the training data, making it harder for the model to help generate something dangerous. DNA is built from four basic building blocks, called bases: A, T, G, and C, standing for Adenine, Thymine, Guanine, and Cytosine. That's really it. That is the entire "alphabet" that all life is written in. A genome is just the full DNA sequence of a living thing. It's basically a very long string made only from these four letters — from a few million letters for a simple bacteria, to over three billion letters for a human. Here's the important part for this audience: one single DNA letter can be treated just like a token in a language model. If you remember, a token is just a small piece of text, like a word or part of a word, that a language model reads one at a time. In DNA, each letter is one token. Its meaning depends on the letters around it, and in theory, you could predict it just from its surroundings, the same way a language model predicts the next word in a sentence. A gene is a piece of the DNA sequence that actually does something useful, kind of like one meaningful sentence hiding inside a very long, mostly boring document. A mutation is just a small change to that string — one letter gets swapped, added, or removed. And just like changing one word in a contract can totally change its meaning, changing one DNA letter in the right spot can break how a gene works, while changing a letter in another spot might do almost nothing.
